results.title: Chelsea Buell: Grocery stores and food deserts in Seattle, Washington
results.description:
According to the CDC, a food desert can be defined as "areas that lack access to affordable fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lowfat milk, and other foods that make up the full range of a healthy diet" (CDC, p. 1).  Food deserts are usually located in areas of low income or in urban or rural areas where smaller convenience stores or restaurants make up the majority of food options.  Those who live within a defined food desert may suffer from low socioeconomic status and health problems like cancer, obesity and other diseases related to diet (USDA, p. 1).  According to Walker et al. on page 877, "a consequence of poor supermarket access is that residents have increased exposure to energy-dense food readily available at convenience stores and fast-food restaurants". 

There are several theories as to how food deserts form and how they affect people.  The first theory "has been associated with both the development and closure of stores" (Walker et al., p.876).  For example, supermarkets may leave the city to follow those migrating to a suburban community.  Also, a Wal-Mart Superstore might push out a competing supermarket as they offer lower prices.  One must be careful however, Wal-Mart may offer cheaper prices but they also offer less healthy options for food.
 
The next theory "pertains to changes in demographics in larger U.S. cities between 1970-1988... this shift caused the median income in the inner-cities to decrease and forced nearly one-half of the supermarkets in the three largest U.S. cities to close" (Walker et al., p. 877).  Mentioned earlier, people who can afford to leave the city often do, and supermarkets follow to suburban localities.  This shift leaves behind people in the cities who are less wealthy and without healthy eating options. 

Looking at the map of grocery store locations in Seattle, Washington, one can see that food deserts do exist in this city.  The neighborhoods in Seattle that seem to be food deserts with the least amount of grocery stores are: 
Broadview, Haller Lake, Lake City, Northgate, North Park, Maple Leaf, Greenwood, Green Lake, Ballard, Phinney Ridge, Wallingford, Magnolia, Queen Anne, Madison Park, Western Seattle, Delridge, Georgetown and White Center. 

Citations:
1) "A Look Inside Food Deserts." Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. September 24, 2012. 
2) "Food Deserts." United States Department of Agriculture. 
3) Walker, Renee E., Christopher R. Keane, Jessica G. Burke. "Disparities and access to healthy food in the United States: A review of food deserts literature." Health & Place 16 (2010) 876-884. 
4) Mela, David J. "Food choice and intake: the human factor." Proceedings of the Nutrition Society (1999) 58: 513-521.
results.snippet: 264 grocery stores are mapped and located in the city of Seattle, displaying zones, or food deserts, without healthy food choices.

results.title: Chelsea Buell: Population Density in Seattle, Washington
results.description:
Studies have been conducted to show a correlation between population density and food deserts.  Those living within the city are usually living in low-income neighborhoods, and therefore have less access to supermarkets.  Supermarkets of specific ethnic origin (Mexican, Middle Eastern, Chinese, etc.) may be more accessible in city centers where highly populated neighborhoods exist, as well as people with lower median household income.  Either supermarkets are not located in the city or those of low-income cannot afford to shop for healthy food.  "... it is often assumed that differential access to neighborhood resources is one explanation for the observed gap in health between deprived and non-deprived neighborhoods" (Pearce et al., p. 349). 

The Seattle neighborhoods with population ranging from 1,001-100,000 people are: 
Broadview, Lake City, Northgate, North Park, Greenwood, Phinney Ridge, Ballard, Wallingford, Green Lake, Queen Anne, Madison Park, Western Seattle, Beacon Hill, Rainier Valley and White Center. 

There seems to be a difference between cities and suburban areas.  In suburban locations, families have left cities and can afford to live in the suburbs, allowing supermarkets to follow these families.  Supermarkets can thrive in suburban locations because these economically successful families can afford the transportation to get to a grocery store of their choice, as well as afford healthy food. 

There also seems to be a correlation between food deserts in rural communities versus urban communities.  Those living in rural areas tend to be less economically successful due to decreased financial opportunities in these rural locations.  Due to rural areas being less wealthy than urban communities, supermarkets are less likely to thrive and therefore will choose a suburban location for their store.  "Accessing healthy food is a challenge for many Americans- particularly those living in low-income neighborhoods, communities of color and rural areas" (Treuhaft & Karpyn, p. 13). 

Citations:
1) Pearce, Jamie, Karen Witten, Rosemary Hiscock, Tony Blakely. "Are socially disadvantaged neighborhoods deprived of health-related community resources?" International Journal of Epidemiology 2007:36:348-355. 
2) Morton, Lois Wrigt, Troy C. Blanchard. "Starved for Access: Life in Rural America's Food Deserts." Rural Realities. Volume 1, Issue 4. 2007. 
3) Treuhaft, Sarah, Allison Karpyn. "The Grocery Gap: Who Has Access to Healthy Food and Why It Matters." Policy Link & The Food Trust. 2010.
results.snippet: Population density within the city of Seattle has a direct correlation to food deserts.

results.title: Chelsea Buell: Median Household Income in Seattle, Washington
results.description:
"The lack of financial resources present a barrier to healthy eating, due to the increased cost associated with healthy eating" (Walker et al., p. 877).  There are several reasons as to why people have poor access to healthy food.  Some may not have access to transportation, single parents may not have the time or extra money to spend on shopping for healthy food, others may not know how to cook and some simply may not be aware of what a balanced diet consists of. 

Socioeconomic status can be measured based on "education, income and occupation" (APA, p.1).  Income can be associated with where a person lives.  If you do not have money, or make very little, then your options for residence, transportation and healthy food are limited.  Also, if one was unable to gain education through high school and college they may not be able to obtain a job that pays enough for residence and food.  "... food prices are higher and food quality is poorer, often inedible, in areas where poverty is the highest, compared to more affluent areas" (Walker et al., p. 880). 

"...dietary patterns and obesity rates vary between neighborhoods, with living in a low-income or deprived area independently associated with the prevalence of obesity and the consumption of a poor diet" (Cummins & Macintyre, p. 100).  Healthy eating can be expensive and some simply cannot afford to eat healthy every week.  For some, healthy eating may be an occasional treat. 
Within the neighborhoods of Seattle, Washington, there are variances of the median household income.  The city center of Seattle has a median household income ranging between $24,000-$39,000, compared to the U.S. median of $50,157.  

The Seattle neighborhoods that have this same $24,000-$39,000 median household range are: 
Broadview, Haller Lake, Lake City, Northgate, North Park, Greenwood, Ballard, Beacon Hill, Mount Baker, Rainier Valley, Georgetown, Delridge and White Center. 
These neighborhoods with lower median household income align with the food deserts in the city of Seattle, Washington. 

Citations:
1) Walker, Renee E., Christopher R. Keane, Jessica G. Burke. "Disparities and access to healthy food in the United States: A review of food deserts literature." Health & Place 16 (2010) 876-884. 
2) "Education & Socioeconomic Status." American Psychological Association.
3) Cummins, Steven, Sally Macintyre. "Food environments and obesity-neighborhood or nation?" International Journal of Epidemiology. 2006:35:100-104.
4) "USDA Defines Food Deserts." American Nutrition Association. Volume 36, No. 3. 2010.
results.snippet: This map portrays the variation of median household income in the city of Seattle in relation to locations of grocery stores.

results.title: Sensitivity of Coastal Environments and Wildlife to Spilled Oil: Puget Sound and Strait of Juan de Fuca, Washington (USA) - Management Areas (Data Basin Dataset)
results.description:
This data set contains polygons that represent the following sensitive human-use management areas in Puget Sound and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Washington: aquaculture sites, commercial fishing areas, Indian reservations, marine sanctuaries, Nature Conservancy areas, national parks, recreational fishing areas, state parks, subsistence areas, wildlife refuges, and other management areas. Location-specific type and source information is stored in relational data tables designed to be used in conjunction with this spatial data layer. This data set comprises a portion of the Environmental Sensitivity Index (ESI) data for Puget Sound and Strait of Juan de Fuca, Washington. ESI data characterize the marine and coastal environments and wildlife by their sensitivity to spilled oil. The ESI data include information for three main components: shoreline habitats, sensitive biological resources, and human-use resources. See also the SOCECON (Socioeconomic Resource Points and Lines) data layer, part of the larger Puget Sound and Strait of Juan de Fuca ESI database, for additional human-use information.
